function.name: get_current_weather
function.description: Retrieve the current weather conditions for a specified location in either Celsius or Fahrenheit. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

location.description: The location for which to retrieve the weather, in the format of 'City, State', such as 'San Francisco, CA' or 'New York, NY'.

unit.description: The unit of measurement for the temperature.

function.name: search_local_docs
function.description: Searches the local knowledge base for documents that match the given natural language query and returns relevant document entries. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search query expressed in natural language, such as 'What are the symptoms of a cold?'.

limit.description: The maximum number of documents to return.

include_metadata.description: Determines whether to include metadata for the documents in the search results.

**First Studio Ghibli film to win the Japan Academy Film Prize for Picture of the Year** | Year | Award ceremony | Winning film | |------|----------------|--------------| | **1998** | 21st Japan Academy Awards (held in 1998 for 1997 releases) | **“Princess Mononoke”** (Japanese title: *Mononoke Hime*) | *Princess Mononoke*, released in Japan on July 12 1997, became the first Ghibli feature to receive the country’s most prestigious film honor – the Japan Academy Prize for Picture of the Year. --- ### How its box‑office success boosted Studio Ghibli’s international popularity | Domestic impact | International impact | |-----------------|----------------------| | • Grossed **¥12.2 billion** (~US$120 million) in Japan, setting a new record for a Japanese animated film at the time.
• Became the highest‑grossing Japanese film of 1997 and remained so until *Spirited Away* (2001). | • Earned roughly **US$20 million** worldwide, with notable earnings in North America, Europe, and Hong Kong.
• Its overseas performance proved that a Japanese anime could resonate with non‑Japanese audiences, encouraging distributors to acquire Ghibli titles for foreign markets. | | • The film’s critical acclaim (including the Japan Academy Award) added prestige to the studio’s brand. | • The award and box‑office success opened doors for a partnership with Walt Disney Studios, who acquired U.S. distribution rights in 2000.
• Disney’s marketing push introduced Ghibli’s storytelling style to a broader Western audience, creating a “Disney‑style” perception of the studio among American viewers. | | • The domestic record‑breaking run demonstrated Ghibli’s ability to produce commercially viable yet artistically ambitious films. | • The success laid the groundwork for future international releases, such as *Spirited Away* (which later won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature), *Howl’s Moving Castle*, and *Ponyo*. | | • The film’s environmental and mythic themes resonated with contemporary social concerns, enhancing its cultural cachet. | • By proving that Ghibli’s narratives could cross cultural boundaries, *Princess Mononoke* encouraged other studios and distributors to take risks on Japanese animation, expanding the global market for anime. | In short, *Princess Mononoke*’s record‑setting domestic box office combined with its respectable overseas earnings and the prestige of the Japan Academy Award created a tipping point. It showed that Studio Ghibli could deliver both artistic depth and commercial success, prompting major distributors (most notably Disney) to bring Ghibli’s catalog to the West and establishing the studio as a household name outside Japan.
